title: Rama breaks
hook: the hero weeps in the forest

segments.voice: Yesterday: the abduction, and Jatayu, the old bird who fought a king and lost his wings. Your line was he tried. Did you think of someone who tried for you? Day fifty-three.

Rama is running. He has chased the golden deer deep into the forest, killed it, and heard it shout in his own voice, and now he's racing back through the trees. On the way he meets Lakshmana coming toward him, alone, and his heart drops. This is the prince who accepted exile in one sentence, who faced fourteen thousand warriors alone, whose face, Valmiki says, didn't change when he lost a kingdom. The brothers reach the clearing together. The hut is there. Sita is not. Today: the steady one, coming apart.
screen: `RACING BACK THROUGH THE TREES.` → `THE STEADY ONE.` → `THE HUT IS EMPTY.`

segments.voice: What happens next doesn't flatter its hero. Rama runs from tree to tree, calling her name, asking the trees whether they've seen her. He asks the river. He asks the deer, and in Valmiki's telling the deer all turn their heads and look south. He weeps until he can barely stand. Then the grief turns into rage. He tells Lakshmana he'll fill the sky with arrows and tear the worlds apart until the gods give her back. It's his younger brother, the one who's usually the hothead, who calms him down: you're the one who taught everyone patience, he says, in effect. Don't become the storm. Then they find Jatayu, and Rama holds the dying bird. So why would a story about a divine hero show him coming apart like this? For Hindus who see Rama as God come to earth as a man, this is part of the point. He took on a human life, and a human life includes losing someone you love. He doesn't skip the grief to get to the rescue. Remember the morning his face didn't change at the news of exile. Losing a kingdom, he stayed still. Losing Sita, he can't. The poem lets you see which loss reached him. And Lakshmana doesn't scold him for it. He stays beside him, and turns him back toward the search. The strongest one in the story breaks, and the poem doesn't think less of him for it.
screen: `RAMA ASKS THE TREES.` · `THE GRIEF TURNS TO RAGE.` · `LAKSHMANA CALMS THE STORM.` · `GOD ON EARTH, AND HE WEEPS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your shoulders drop. Think of a strong person in your life who is grieving something right now, or who grieved in front of you once. Don't try to fix it. Don't try to cheer them up. Just sit next to them in your mind, the way Lakshmana sits next to Rama. Let their sadness be there without rushing it along. If something of your own grief comes up, let it sit there too. Nobody has to be the strong one for two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Rama breaks. The hero, in the empty forest, asking the trees where she went. The poem doesn't hide it.
Your line: even he wept. Today, if someone strong near you looks tired, don't ask them to be strong. Ask how they are, and wait for the real answer. Day fifty-three.

howItsDone: Rama's lament in the forest is recited and sung in Ramayana readings, and Ramlila performances often stage it as an emotional scene; many devotees speak of Rama's grief as part of his fully human life on earth.

fork.setup: you're Lakshmana. your brother is weeping, then swearing he'll tear the worlds apart with arrows. what do you do?

remind him who he is, and calm him.
leave him alone until it passes.
fork.reveal: Lakshmana, usually the hothead, becomes the calm one: he reminds Rama of his own patience and turns him back toward the search.

original.note: Sanskrit: lament, weeping aloud; Rama's lament in the forest.

trapdoor: what you thought: heroes don't cry.
what it means: Rama, whom his devotees see as God on earth, weeps and rages in the forest, and the poem doesn't hide it.
what a scholar hears: Valmiki gives the lament at length: Rama questions the trees and the river, the deer look south, and Lakshmana, usually the fierce brother, counsels patience.
